name: Metadata and Ontologies
title: Metadata and Ontologies
answer: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories cover the structured descriptions that make datasets, papers, models and tools findable, comparable and reusable. This includes descriptive, administrative and structural metadata, plus formal ontologies that define classes, properties and relationships within a domain. The work sits at the boundary between library science, knowledge engineering and data curation. It supports discovery, citation, provenance tracking and machine readability across scholarly outputs.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories cover the structured descriptions that make datasets, papers, models and tools findable, comparable and reusable. This includes descriptive, administrative and structural metadata, plus formal ontologies that define classes, properties and relationships within a domain. The work sits at the boundary between library science, knowledge engineering and data curation. It supports discovery, citation, provenance tracking and machine readability across scholarly outputs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure runs on repository software, cataloguing systems, graph databases and linked data stores. Metadata records are typically expressed in schemas such as Dublin Core, DataCite, Schema.org or domain specific profiles, while ontologies are encoded in RDF, OWL or SKOS. These systems often sit behind APIs and harvesters that aggregate records from many institutional and disciplinary repositories. The site's own library of 135 research papers and 11222 extracted claims relies on this kind of structured indexing to connect papers to models, tools and glossary terms.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a mix of manual curation, automated extraction and community standard setting. Curators map fields from source systems to shared schemas, reconcile terms against controlled vocabularies, and resolve conflicts between overlapping ontologies. Machine learning assists with entity recognition, topic classification and suggestion of candidate terms, but human review remains central for quality and domain nuance. Versioning and change management are handled through governance processes that document every term addition, deprecation or mapping change.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in metadata and ontologies centre on provenance, bias and control. A term or classification can encode a particular worldview, and poorly maintained mappings can silently misrepresent a dataset or research claim. Repositories therefore keep provenance records showing who created or changed a term, when, and under what authority. Licensing of vocabularies and metadata records also matters, since some ontologies carry restrictions that affect reuse. The site links to original papers rather than to a search tool, which keeps the provenance chain from claim to source intact.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward richer semantic layers that connect research objects across repositories without requiring a single universal schema. Expect more use of knowledge graphs, persistent identifiers and machine actionable data management plans. Ontology alignment and automated metadata generation will improve, but the need for transparent, community governed vocabularies will grow as AI systems consume research data at scale. The practical goal is not one perfect ontology but interoperable, well documented mappings that preserve context.
